title: Panja Sahib
hook: the gurdwara of the handprint at Hasan Abdal

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kartarpur Sahib, where Guru Nanak farmed, and his hymn of the mind as farmer and the body as field. Your line was where he farmed. What work did you do slowly with your hands? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-one.

Clear water slides out from under a rock, into a stone channel, and on into a wide tank where fish turn lazily in the light. A line of pilgrims waits along the edge. One by one, each kneels, reaches out, and fits a hand into a shape pressed into the rock above the water. Some hold it there a long moment. Some laugh because their hand is smaller. Some close their eyes. This is Hasan Abdal, in the hills of northern Pakistan, and the gurdwara is Panja Sahib. Year one told the story of the rock. Today, the water.
screen: `WATER FROM UNDER A ROCK.` → `A HAND FITTED INTO STONE.` → `TODAY, THE WATER.`

segments.voice: First, the story in one breath, because year one told it in full. Tradition says Guru Nanak and Mardana came to the hill thirsty. Mardana climbed three times to ask for water from the spring of a holy man at the top, Wali Qandhari, and three times came down with nothing. Nanak had him lift a stone at the foot of the hill, and water came up. A boulder came rolling down. Nanak stopped it with his open palm, and his hand, the story says, stayed in the stone. Panja means the palm of the hand. Second, look at where the water went. It was refused at the top. It came up at the bottom, where the thirsty men were sitting. And it's still flowing at the bottom today, under the handprint, through the tank, past the pilgrims. Third, a line that explains why water matters so much in this story. In the Japji, Guru Nanak says, here in paraphrase, that the Guru has given him one understanding: there is one giver for every living being, and may he never forget that one. Water is about as plain a gift as there is. In the story, nobody owns the giver. Fourth, how to hold the hilltop. Sikhs read this story in more than one way, some as a miracle, some as a picture. And people remember Wali Qandhari differently from the story; a shrine to him still stands on the hill above, and visitors climb to it too. So the place keeps both: a shrine on the hill, a gurdwara at its foot, and water running between. What the story leaves a pilgrim is the shape of the hand: open, steady, at the place where the thirsty were given a drink. That's today's line: the handprint.
screen: `THREE CLIMBS, AND NOTHING.` · `REFUSED ABOVE, RISING BELOW.` · `ONE GIVER FOR EVERY LIVING BEING.` · `A SHRINE ABOVE, A GURDWARA BELOW.` · then, large: `THE HANDPRINT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put your palm flat. Settle, and breathe. Lay one hand flat on a table, your knee, or the floor. Feel the whole palm touching, the fingers spread, nothing gripped. Breathe in and notice the hand is steady. Breathe out and notice it's open. Now think of someone who's thirsty for something you could give, time, a call, a glass of water, a kind word. Keep the palm open while you think of them. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Panja Sahib. The gurdwara at Hasan Abdal where pilgrims fit their hands into the print of Guru Nanak's palm, with water flowing beneath it. Today's word.
Your line: the handprint. Today, give someone a drink without being asked: a glass of water, a cup of tea, a bottle handed across. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Pilgrims who visit Gurdwara Panja Sahib at Hasan Abdal place their hands in the handprint on the rock and take water from the spring that flows beneath it.

myth: at Panja Sahib the water flows from the top of the hill
in the story it was refused above and came up below, and it still flows under the handprint.
pilgrims fit their hands into the print on the rock
they kneel at the water's edge and place a hand in the shape.
the hilltop shrine to Wali Qandhari is gone
it still stands on the hill above the gurdwara, and visitors climb to it too.

fork.setup: you're Mardana. three times you've climbed for water and come down with nothing. Nanak tells you to lift a stone at the foot of the hill. what comes up?
options: a coin to buy a drink.
fork.reveal: tradition says water came up from under the stone, at the bottom of the hill where the thirsty men were. it still flows there today.

original.note: panja, the palm of the hand: the gurdwara named for the handprint in the rock.

trapdoor: what you thought: the gurdwara with the famous handprint.
what it means: a place where water refused at the top came up at the bottom, and still flows under an open palm.
what a scholar hears: the story comes from later tradition, not the Granth; the place keeps both a shrine on the hill and a gurdwara below.
recall: a mint, where coins are struck
one on the path of seva

notes: Day 38 told the story in full (including the open palm and a palm-on-the-wall practice) and day 988 told the 1922 train. Today's angle is the water: refused above, rising below, still flowing. The outline's practice ('put your palm flat') overlaps day 38's; the practice here is turned toward giving.

Fairness: Wali Qandhari is not cast as a villain beyond what the story says; the voice notes that people remember him differently and that his hilltop shrine still stands. A Keeper and ideally a Muslim reader should check the wording.
Hook details (fish in the tank, pilgrims fitting their hands into the print): please confirm.
